Latest Update: What Are Mutual Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1670 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, if you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list.
  • This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.
  • Recent findings suggest that A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you have ever looked at your 401(k) options or browsed a brokerage account, you have almost certainly seen mutual funds on the list. They are one of the most widely used investment vehicles in the country, and for good reason. But not all mutual funds are built the same, and understanding the differences can have a real impact on how much money you actually keep over time.

This article breaks down what mutual funds are, how they work, the different types you will encounter, and what to watch out for when deciding whether one belongs in your portfolio.

Recent findings suggest that A mutual fund is a pooled investment vehicle. When you invest in a mutual fund, your money is combined with money from thousands of other investors. A fund manager then uses that pool of capital to buy a collection of assets, which might include stocks, bonds, or a mix of both, depending on the fund’s objective.

It has been revealed that each investor owns shares of the mutual fund, and those shares represent a proportional stake in everything the fund holds. When the underlying assets increase in value, your shares go up. When they fall, your shares go down.

Industry observers note that mutual funds are priced once per day, after the market closes, based on the total value of all the assets inside the fund. This is called the net asset value, or NAV. Unlike stocks, which trade throughout the day at constantly changing prices, mutual fund transactions are always settled at the end-of-day price.

Sources indicate that when you buy shares of a mutual fund, you are not picking individual stocks or bonds yourself. Instead, you are hiring a fund manager, or a team of them, to make those decisions on your behalf. The fund follows a stated investment objective, and the manager selects holdings that align with that goal.

For example, a fund that aims for long-term growth might hold primarily large-cap U.S. stocks. A fund focused on income might hold a mix of dividend-paying stocks and bonds. The fund’s prospectus, a document you can access before investing, spells out exactly what the fund is trying to do and how it looks to do it.

According to recent reports, investors buy and sell mutual fund shares directly through the fund manufacturer or through a brokerage account. You can invest a specific dollar amount rather than buying a whole number of shares, making them accessible to investors at just about any level.

There are thousands of mutual funds available, but most fall into a handful of broad categories.

These funds invest primarily in stocks. They can be further broken down by the size of the companies they hold (large-cap, mid-cap, small-cap), the style of investing (growth vs. value), or the geography (U.S. only, international, or global). Stock funds carry more risk than bond funds but also offer greater long-term growth potential.

Bond funds (fixed income funds).

Bond funds hold debt securities issued by governments, corporations, or municipalities. They are generally considered less volatile than stock funds and are often used to add stability to a portfolio. However, they also tend to produce lower returns over long periods.

It has been revealed that these funds hold a combination of stocks and bonds within a single fund. The allocation varies by fund, but the idea is to provide both growth and income while smoothing out some of the volatility of a pure stock fund.

Money market funds invest in short-term, low-risk debt instruments. They aim to maintain a stable value and are often used as a place to park cash. The returns are modest, and they are not a long-term wealth-building strategy.

Index funds are a specific type of mutual fund that tracks a market index, such as the S&P 500, rather than relying on active stock picking. Because they are passively managed, they tend to have much lower fees than other types of mutual funds. Over the long run, they have consistently outperformed most actively managed alternatives after costs are taken into account.

This distinction is one of the most vital things to understand about mutual funds, and it directly affects your returns.

An actively managed fund employs a portfolio manager who researches investments, makes judgment calls, and trades frequently to outperform the market. This sounds appealing. Who would not want a professional trying to beat the market on their behalf?

According to recent reports, the problem is that most actively managed funds do not beat the market over the long run, especially after fees are factored in. Study after study over multiple decades has shown that the majority of active fund managers underperform a simple index fund over a ten-year period. Yet they charge significantly more for the attempt.

A passively managed fund, like an index fund, does not try to beat the market. It simply tracks it. The holdings change only when the underlying index changes. Because no active management is required, the fees are a fraction of those charged by actively managed funds.

Recent findings suggest that for most long-term investors, a low-cost index fund is the better choice. The math is straightforward: lower fees mean more of your return stays in your pocket, and that difference compounds significantly over decades.

Fees are one of the most overlooked factors in investing, and they deserve your full attention. Here are the main ones to know.

It has been revealed that the expense ratio is the annual cost of owning a fund, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A fund with a 1.00% expense ratio costs you $10 per year for every $1,000 you have invested. That may sound small, but over 30 years of investing, that difference compared to a fund charging 0.05% can amount to tens of thousands of dollars.

Some mutual funds charge a sales commission, called a load, either when you buy (front-end load) or when you sell (back-end load). A front-end load of 5% means that only $950 of every $1,000 you invest actually goes into the fund. There is no reason to pay a sales load when thousands of excellent no-load funds are available.

Recent findings suggest that these are marketing and distribution fees charged by some funds. They are baked into the expense ratio and can add up. A fund with a high 12b-1 fee is often a sign that the fund is spending money on sales and marketing rather than managing your investment.

In a recent development, when you invest in a mutual fund, you immediately own a small piece of every asset the fund holds. A single investment gives you exposure to hundreds or even thousands of companies, which spreads your risk far more effectively than buying individual stocks ever could.

According to recent reports, for investors who do not want to research individual securities, mutual funds hand the decision-making over to professionals. This is especially relevant for bond funds and specialty funds, where the research involved is more complex than evaluating stocks.

Most mutual funds have low minimum investment requirements, and many allow you to invest in dollar amounts rather than whole shares. This makes them a practical option for investors who are just getting started or working with a limited budget.

It has been revealed that mutual funds in the United States are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Commission. Fund companies are required to disclose their holdings, fees, and performance data regularly. That transparency makes it relatively easy to compare options and know exactly what you are getting into.

Fees can erode your returns significantly.

Recent findings suggest that this is the biggest concern with many mutual funds, particularly actively managed ones. High expense ratios and sales loads reduce your effective return every single year. Over a long investing horizon, that drag is substantial. Always check the expense ratio before investing in any fund.

According to recent reports, because mutual funds are priced once daily at market close, you cannot buy or sell during trading hours at a live price. For long-term investors, this is rarely a concern. But it is worth understanding how mutual funds differ from ETFs in this regard.

In a recent development, when a mutual fund sells holdings at a profit, it distributes those capital gains to shareholders at the end of the year. Even if you did not sell any of your own shares, you may owe taxes on those distributions. This is less of an concern in tax-advantaged accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, but it is something to keep in mind for taxable brokerage accounts.

In a recent development, it is possible to hold too many mutual funds that overlap in their holdings, leaving you with a bloated, redundant portfolio. Owning five different large-cap U.S. stock funds does not give you five times the diversification. It mostly just gives you five sets of fees.

Recent findings suggest that with thousands of mutual funds available, narrowing down your options does not have to be complicated. A few straightforward criteria will get you most of the way there.

Sources indicate that mutual funds are among the most practical investments available to everyday investors. They make it easy to build a diversified portfolio without needing to research and manage individual securities. For most people, the primary vehicle for building wealth over time is a 401(k), IRA, or taxable brokerage account.

Industry observers note that that said, not all mutual funds are worth your money. Actively managed funds and those with high sales loads or steep expense ratios consistently underperform lower-cost alternatives over the long run. The evidence strongly favors low-cost index funds as the core of most investors’ portfolios.

The most key step is to start. Aim to invest at least 10% of your gross income consistently, keep your costs low, stay diversified, and give your money time to grow. The mechanics of which specific funds you choose matter far less than the discipline of contributing regularly over many years.

Latest Update: Health Sharing vs. Traditional Health Insurance: Which Is Right for You?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A health sharing plan (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance organization.
  • It has been revealed that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing plans have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

A health sharing plan (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance organization. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

It has been revealed that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA looks, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Read our review of Zion HealthShare.

According to recent reports, traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace plan, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Recent findings suggest that solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health proposal with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

According to recent reports, employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace looks are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

Industry observers note that but that gap exists because health sharing plans aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

It works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

Health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

In a recent development, is a health sharing proposal the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing strategy and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing initiative cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

It has been revealed that online stores reprice items as demand, stock, and rivals’ prices change, and some also use your location or browsing history to set the price you see. Before you buy, check the item at another store and in a logged-out private window, then set a price alert instead of guessing when the price will drop.

Industry observers note that from one screen, you can’t tell whether a price jumped for every shopper or just for you. Both happen, and the second has been documented for over a decade.

In 2012, The Wall Street Journal found Staples’ website showing one shopper a stapler for $15.79 and another, a few miles away, the same stapler for $14.29. The lower price usually went to shoppers the site judged to be within about 20 miles of an OfficeMax or Office Depot store. In January 2025, the Federal Trade Commission published first findings from its study of the firms retailers hire to set prices. Details like your precise location or browsing history can often be used to give you a different price than other shoppers get for the same goods, the agency found.

In Upcoming York, the Algorithmic Pricing Disclosure Act requires a store that sets a price from your personal data to say so with the notice “This price was set by an algorithm using your personal data.” Since Oct. 1, 2026, a Maryland law has barred large grocers and grocery delivery services from using personal data to charge shoppers more for groceries.

According to recent reports, A price alert beats refreshing the page, since you can’t predict when software working from data you never see will cut the price. Google Shopping’s price tracking emails you when the price drops below a target you choose, so base that target on the item’s price history.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The cheaper bag of pet food isn’t always the cheaper one to feed.
  • According to recent reports, the price per pound on a shelf tag misses how long each pound lasts.
  • Take two 30-pound bags for a 50-pound dog, at illustrative prices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The cheaper bag of pet food isn’t always the cheaper one to feed. A denser food holds more calories in each cup, so your pet eats less of it and the bag lasts longer. Before you buy or switch, divide each bag’s price by the days it lasts at your pet’s feeding amount.

According to recent reports, the price per pound on a shelf tag misses how long each pound lasts. A pound of a calorie-dense food feeds your pet for more days than a pound of a less dense one.

Take two 30-pound bags for a 50-pound dog, at illustrative prices. One costs $45 and lasts the dog 40 days. The other, a denser food, costs $52 and lasts 47 days. Per pound, the denser food costs $1.73 and the other $1.50. Per day, the denser food costs about $1.11 and the other about $1.13, so the $52 bag costs less to feed than the $45 bag.

Recent findings suggest that gaps like that grow with how much your pet eats, so they matter most for substantial dogs. A gap of 10 cents a day comes to $36.50 a year.

To compare two dry foods this way:.

Newer labels list a cup’s weight in grams instead of kcal/kg. To get kcal/kg from those, multiply the calories per cup by 1,000 and divide by that weight. For canned food, divide your pet’s daily calories by the calories per can, then multiply by the price per can.

Between two sizes of the same food, every pound holds the same calories, so the lower price per pound settles it. The bigger bag’s saving depends on the food staying fresh. A veterinary nutritionist at Tufts University recommends finishing an opened bag within two to three months, so buy the size your pet empties in that time.

Industry observers note that switch to a fresh food slowly. Mix a little more of it into the old food each day for at least a week.

How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2054 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Congratulations!
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun newly introduced way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,.

Recent findings suggest that “Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

Industry observers note that one of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

Recent findings suggest that I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

It has been revealed that I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Sources indicate that then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

According to recent reports, during the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

But eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Sources indicate that admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Recent findings suggest that then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

It has been revealed that it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning latest things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

In a recent development, one interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

So I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

Industry observers note that thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

Industry observers note that so here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

It has been revealed that and of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

But I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

Industry observers note that as with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

Industry observers note that we will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

Avianca LifeMiles → Star Alliance Premium Cabin

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One of the cheapest ways to fly Star Alliance business and first class.
  • Picture this: you settle into a Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 business class seat on the upper deck, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, your fully flat bed already made up behind you.
  • The core insight here is understanding why Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards so aggressively — and then understanding how to get points into the program quickly enough to actually use them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One of the cheapest ways to fly Star Alliance business and first class.

Points for Business/First Class.

Picture this: you settle into a Lufthansa Boeing 747-8 business class seat on the upper deck, somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of Champagne in hand, your fully flat bed already made up behind you. Latest York to Frankfurt — a route that commands $4,000 to $8,000 in cash for a business class ticket — and you're here for 63,000 Avianca LifeMiles. No fuel surcharges. No carrier-imposed fees eating into your redemption. Just the experience. That's the moment the FI community lives for. Not the luxury itself — though Lufthansa's business class product is genuinely exceptional — but the *math*. The realization that the loyalty system has a pricing gap so wide you could fly a 747 through it. Here's what the numbers actually mean. At the low end, a $4,000 business class ticket redeemed for 63,000 points works out to **6.3 cents per point (CPP)**. At the high end — peak travel season, last-minute pricing, transatlantic demand — that same seat hits $8,000 in cash, which means your LifeMiles are delivering **12.7 cents per point**. For context, most travel rewards experts consider 1–2 CPP a baseline for points value. You're achieving 6 to 12 times that baseline. The reason this feels like a genuine inefficiency rather than just a deal: Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards on a **fixed award chart** that doesn't fluctuate with cash fare demand. When airlines raise transatlantic business class fares during summer holidays or major events, your points cost stays exactly the same. The gap between what the market charges and what LifeMiles charges simply grows wider. And then there's the no-fuel-surcharge policy — the detail that separates LifeMiles from competitors like British Airways Avios, which can pile $600+ in carrier surcharges onto a single redemption. With LifeMiles, you pay government taxes only, typically $50–$150 for a transatlantic itinerary. That's it. For the ChooseFI community, this redemption represents exactly the kind of asymmetric value that underpins a great travel rewards strategy: use points where cash prices are highest, eliminate fees wherever possible, and fly a product you'd never justify paying full price for — because you didn't have to.

The core insight here is understanding why Avianca LifeMiles prices Star Alliance awards so aggressively — and then understanding how to get points into the program quickly enough to actually use them.

Sources indicate that avianca is a Star Alliance member, which means it has reciprocal award booking agreements with every other Star Alliance carrier — United, Lufthansa, Swiss, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines, and more. Like all alliance programs, LifeMiles can sell award seats on partner airlines. The pricing is set by Avianca's own award chart, not by Lufthansa's chart or United's chart.

This is the pricing inefficiency. Lufthansa's own frequent flyer program (Miles & More) charges over 100,000 miles for the same transatlantic business class route and layers on fuel surcharges. United MileagePlus charges 70,000–88,000 miles for the same seat. Avianca LifeMiles charges 63,000 miles with zero carrier surcharges. Same seat. Same plane. Wildly different cost.

Avianca keeps rates competitive because they want their program to be attractive to non-Avianca flyers — it's a revenue play. And because their route network is South America-focused, they've built a powerful award program that earns loyalty from customers who may never set foot on an Avianca plane.

Many programs claim no surcharges, then quietly pass through "carrier-imposed fees" that look indistinguishable from surcharges. LifeMiles is one of the genuine exceptions. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A Walmart clearance sticker keeps the price it was printed with, and the store may have marked the item down again since.
  • Walmart says each store’s manager can cut prices to clear out extra stock, and that changing prices on paper tags by hand could take hours or even days.
  • Walmart is replacing its paper shelf tags with digital labels that show the same price the register charges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A Walmart clearance sticker keeps the price it was printed with, and the store may have marked the item down again since. Scan the item with the free Walmart app while you’re in the store. The app shows that store’s current price, and that’s what you’ll pay at the register.

Walmart says each store’s manager can cut prices to clear out extra stock, and that changing prices on paper tags by hand could take hours or even days. The register charges the latest price in the meantime.

Walmart is replacing its paper shelf tags with digital labels that show the same price the register charges. It said in March 2026 that it expects every U.S. store to have them within a year. A clearance sticker on the item itself is still paper, though, so it’s the likeliest place to find an old price, along with the shelf tags in any store that hasn’t switched yet.

Say a pair of kids’ sneakers carries a $14.97 clearance sticker, and the store has since cut the price to $5. The sticker still indicates $14.97, but the app indicates $5, and $5 is what you’ll pay.

Look for clearance stickers on the displays at the ends of aisles, along the back wall of each department, and in the seasonal aisle the week after a holiday. Open the app inside the store with location sharing on, since it shows in-store prices only once it knows you’re there. Then tap the scanner icon in the search bar and scan the product’s own barcode, not one printed for shipping or storage.

In a recent development, the price you see applies only at that store. Walmart claims prices can vary from store to store and that it doesn’t price match its own stores, so the store won’t match a lower price you found at another Walmart. Clearance is also whatever the store has left, so an item you pass up today may be gone the next time you come in.

For a significant purchase you can time, like a TV or a mattress, skip the clearance hunt and wait for its category’s yearly sale season.

Scan every clearance sticker before the item goes in your cart, and buy what scans at a price you’d pay.

Download the free Walmart app and sign in before your next trip.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you buy a print book fresh, look for a used copy, which often costs a few dollars.
  • Recent findings suggest that A hardcover that costs $30 new can cost $2 at a library sale or $6 with shipping from an online used-book seller.
  • Industry observers note that online, the catch is shipping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you buy a print book fresh, look for a used copy, which often costs a few dollars. Online, compare sellers by what you’d pay with shipping, not the listed price. Then check library book sales near you, where many books cost even less.

Recent findings suggest that A hardcover that costs $30 new can cost $2 at a library sale or $6 with shipping from an online used-book seller. Books hold up well, so a used copy in good condition reads just like a new one.

Industry observers note that online, the catch is shipping. On a marketplace like AbeBooks, each seller sets its own shipping charge, so a $1 copy with $4 shipping costs more than a $4 copy that ships free. BookFinder.com compares offers from more than 100,000 booksellers, and its searches take shipping into account. Search the title there before you buy anywhere.

ThriftBooks, which sells millions of used books, charges nothing for standard shipping on a US order over $15, so buying several books at once can cost less than ordering them one at a time.

Locally, browse used bookstores and thrift stores, and watch for library book sales. The library’s Friends group, which raises money for the library, often runs the sale, and hardcovers commonly cost $1 to $3. Many end with a bag sale, when a full bag often costs $5 or $10. Find one on your library’s website or on Book Sale Finder, which lists library and other nonprofit book sales by state. Some libraries also keep a sale shelf or a Friends bookstore open between sales.

Before you pay, check the condition grade. ThriftBooks’ grades run from Like New down to Acceptable, and AbeBooks’ guide describes a Good copy as one with average wear and every text page intact. That’s usually good enough for a book you’ll read rather than display. Ex-library copies, former library books that often carry stamps and stickers, usually cost less. To get a particular edition, search by its ISBN, the number assigned to each edition and format of a book. A hardcover and a paperback of the same title each have their own.

Trade in the books you won’t reread at a used bookstore that buys them, and ask for store credit, which is often worth at least 20% more than the cash offer.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Systeme.io has burst onto the digital marketing scene, brandishing a bold claim as an all-in-one, free platform.

Let’s face it, when you hear something like that, your first thought is, “This has got to be too good to be true.”.

Recent findings suggest that that was my initial reaction too. A free, do-it-all software that doesn’t suck? Highly doubtful.

But here’s the shocker: Systeme.io isn’t just blowing smoke. It’s a game-changer. As someone who’s navigated the maze of digital marketing tools, I was prepared for disappointment. Yet, Systeme.io left me floored with its capabilities.

According to recent reports, take it from someone who’s been around the block with the likes of ConvertKit, AWeber, and MailChimp. These giants lure you in with free offerings, only to tighten the screws when your audience grows. Cheaper Pet Food Can Be as Complete as Premium – Check the AAFCO Statement

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before paying extra for premium dog or cat food, find the small-print line on the package that names your pet’s life stage and AAFCO, the group that sets pet food nutrient standards.
  • In each food’s biggest bag at Walmart, the store’s own Pure Balance Chicken & Brown Rice Recipe costs $1.17 a pound, less than half the $2.67 a pound for Blue Buffalo’s Wilderness Grain-Free Chicken Recipe.
  • That line is the nutritional adequacy statement, and newer labels add a short version on the front, such as Complete Food for Adult Dogs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before paying extra for premium dog or cat food, find the small-print line on the package that names your pet’s life stage and AAFCO, the group that sets pet food nutrient standards. Any food with that line meets the same standards as pricier brands, so buy the cheapest one your pet does well on.

In each food’s biggest bag at Walmart, the store’s own Pure Balance Chicken & Brown Rice Recipe costs $1.17 a pound, less than half the $2.67 a pound for Blue Buffalo’s Wilderness Grain-Free Chicken Recipe. Both dry dog foods carry that line and have nearly the same calories per pound.

That line is the nutritional adequacy statement, and newer labels add a short version on the front, such as Complete Food for Adult Dogs. The statement claims the food was formulated to meet the nutrient standards of the Association of American Feed Control Officials (AAFCO) or passed AAFCO feeding trials. It also names a life stage, such as growth for puppies and kittens, adult maintenance, or all life stages. The FDA says a food has to pass one of those tests to be called complete and balanced, which means it’s meant to be your pet’s only food. One labeled for intermittent or supplemental feeding only isn’t a complete diet.

Premium claims don’t make a food more complete. Natural describes how ingredients are sourced and processed, organic how they’re grown, and human-grade how the food and its ingredients are handled. Grain-free isn’t healthier for most pets either. Veterinary nutritionists at Tufts University call it a marketing concept and say grain allergies are rare.

In a recent development, the FDA has also investigated reports of a heart disease called dilated cardiomyopathy in dogs eating certain foods, many of them grain-free. It hasn’t established that the foods cause the disease, but ask your vet before switching your dog to grain-free.

It has been revealed that so compare prices only among foods whose statement names your pet’s life stage, and look at dry food first. In a Tufts price check of cat foods, even the most expensive dry food cost less per day than the cheapest canned one, for the same calories.

If you’d rather cook, have a veterinary nutritionist write the recipe for any homemade dog food or cat food you’d serve daily.

For a grown dog or cat, a store brand whose statement covers adult maintenance or all life stages is a complete diet.

Amazon Resale Sells Returns for Less – Check What the Grade Indicates Is Missing

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (495 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Before you buy a bigger item fresh on Amazon, check Amazon Resale, formerly Amazon Warehouse.
  • One product can be listed on Resale in several grades at once, each at its own price.
  • Amazon inspects each item before giving it one of four grades, and it tests electronics and resets them to factory settings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you buy a bigger item fresh on Amazon, check Amazon Resale, formerly Amazon Warehouse. Amazon sells inspected returns and open-box goods there below the new price, with its usual return policy. Read the condition grade first, since a lower grade can mean missing accessories or parts, and buy only when the discount covers their cost.

One product can be listed on Resale in several grades at once, each at its own price.

Amazon inspects each item before giving it one of four grades, and it tests electronics and resets them to factory settings. A Like New item works perfectly and has every essential accessory, though its packaging may be damaged. A Very Good one may show light use and minor cosmetic flaws, and it can lack non-essential accessories.

In a recent development, A Good item can show wear from moderate use, and an Acceptable one can show clear signs of use, such as scratches and dents. Either may be missing accessories or parts you’d have to buy before you can use it, and the listing’s description names anything missing.

To find offers, browse Amazon Resale by category, or look on a regular product page for the Save with Used or Buy Used section and open See details to compare grades. Resale purchases fall under Amazon’s return policy, which gives most items 30 days. Each item is one of a kind, though, so Amazon can’t swap a disappointing one for another in exactly the same condition. Test your item the day it arrives.

In a recent development, check the maker’s warranty too. Under FTC rules, a written warranty on a product over $15 must say so if it covers only the original buyer, which may not be you. For a laptop or phone you’d want covered by a warranty, look at refurbished electronics sold with one instead.

According to recent reports, say a stand mixer is listed as Like Fresh at 20% below the new price because a buyer opened the box and sent it back. Every essential accessory is included, so you get a fully working mixer for 20% less, in an opened box. At a lower grade with the bowl missing, the discount has to cover a new bowl before it saves you anything.

Like New and Very Good are the grades to start with, since neither can be missing anything the item needs to work.

Search Amazon Resale for the next bigger item on your shopping list.

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your credit report lists your loans and cards with their balances, limits, and payment history, plus any collections, any bankruptcy, and the companies that have checked it.
  • Sources indicate that lenders read that report before they approve you or set your rate, and landlords, insurers, and phone companies can check it too.
  • It has been revealed that the report covers credit only.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your credit report lists your loans and cards with their balances, limits, and payment history, plus any collections, any bankruptcy, and the companies that have checked it. Your income, savings, and credit score aren’t on it. Pull your free reports and read each section for accounts you didn’t open, wrong balances, and on-time payments marked late.

Sources indicate that lenders read that report before they approve you or set your rate, and landlords, insurers, and phone companies can check it too. Seeing it first lets you catch a mistake before it costs you.

It has been revealed that the report covers credit only. Paying with a debit card isn’t borrowing, so that spending normally doesn’t show up. Your score is calculated from the report but isn’t part of it. Since April 2023, the three credit bureaus have also stopped listing any medical bill sent to collectors that’s been paid off, was under $500 when first reported, or is less than a year past due.

Recent findings suggest that negative items don’t stay for good. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes most, like late payments, can be reported for up to seven years, and a bankruptcy for up to 10.

Read each of your free reports one section at a time:.

In a recent development, not every surprise is a problem. A first-time reader might find a store card she forgot, still open at a $0 balance. That card has been helping her, since an open account with no missed payments keeps adding to the length of her credit history.

Dispute any entry that’s wrong, not just forgotten.

Checking your own reports never lowers your score, so read them now, well before a lender does.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that clean your car inside and out yourself in an afternoon, with about $40 in supplies. Wash it in the shade with car soap and two buckets, then vacuum and treat cloth seats and carpet with baking soda and diluted vinegar. Save a pro detail for paint scratches, stubborn stains or smells, and a car you’re about to sell.

Industry observers note that consumer Reports notes to expect to pay more than $200 to have a car deep-cleaned inside and out. Neither the wash nor the wipe-down needs pro equipment.

Fill one bucket with water and car wash soap, not dish soap, which Consumer Reports warns may strip off the protective wax. Rinse your wash mitt in a second bucket of plain water after each section, so the grit doesn’t scratch the paint.

Wash in the shade from the roof down, since sun can dry the soap into spots before you rinse it. Then dry with microfiber towels, because air-drying can leave mineral spots.

It has been revealed that about $40 buys two 5-gallon buckets, car wash soap, a wash mitt, microfiber towels, a dashboard protectant, and an ammonia-free glass cleaner, since ammonia can damage window tint film. Add baking soda and white vinegar from the kitchen, and do the inside in this order.

Leave three jobs to a detailer. Paint correction, which removes scratches and swirl marks, needs a pro’s tools and experience. Stains or smells that outlast the baking soda and vinegar need a detailer’s hot-water carpet cleaner or odor treatment. And before you sell, book a detail only when it costs less than it adds to your car’s resale value.

Say four $200 details a year cost you $800 and one $40 kit lasts the year. Doing it yourself saves $760 of that $800, or $190 for each afternoon of work.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.
  • But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here.
  • It has been revealed that I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

It has been revealed that I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

Industry observers note that but a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,.

“But I’m still gonna keep fighting it!”.

According to recent reports, yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

Recent findings suggest that one of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder. And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

Recent findings suggest that so I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new manufacturer, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:.

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

Sources indicate that and wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

In a recent development, it’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

Recent findings suggest that in many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

But there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

It has been revealed that while this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me).

According to recent reports, distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

Sources indicate that and while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

In a recent development, so I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

It has been revealed that I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty swiftly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”.

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”.

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

So Why Doesn’t Everyone Do This?

According to recent reports, when you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that notes, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the matter, you’ll see this:.

Stuff you should do BEFORE trying TRT:.

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

According to recent reports, since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

According to recent reports, more modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

Recent findings suggest that my hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

And it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower.

Industry observers note that the great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The tech giant that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

It has been revealed that note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Read the number in the top-right corner of a Target clearance sticker. It’s the percentage off, and most clearance drops from 30% to 50% to 70%. Wait for 70% when the shelf is full, and buy now when only a few are left in the size or color you want.

In a recent development, A $40 lamp tagged 30% off costs $28 today and $12 at 70% off, so waiting saves $16 if it’s still on the shelf. Anyone else can buy it in the meantime.

Most items go on clearance at 30% off, and everyday food at 15%. Household basics tend to sell out before they reach 70%. A date near the bottom of the sticker tells you when the current price took effect.

Seventy percent is the last step for most clearance, and Target pulls what’s left from the shelves soon after. Holiday decorations and gifts drop faster and can go on to 90%. Each store sets its own timing, so the dates on your store’s stickers tell you more than any day-by-department schedule posted online.

Sources indicate that scan the barcode in the Target app before you decide. Stores can take days to put up newly introduced stickers, so an item can ring up at a deeper markdown than its sticker shows.

It has been revealed that the deeper markdown is worth waiting for on anything the store has plenty of. When the shelf is down to one or two in your size or color, buy at 30% or 50%, since waiting saves nothing on an item that’s gone. Target’s price match excludes clearance, so you can’t get the difference back after a later markdown.

Industry observers note that the day after Christmas, holiday lights at 50% off usually reach 70% within the week and 90% soon after, while a popular toy at 30% off can sell out before its next markdown. Hold off on the lights, and buy the toy now.

Regular clearance typically drops again about two weeks after the date on its sticker, so strategy your next trip for that week.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Trade the books you’ve finished for ones you haven’t read. A Little Free Library box or a swap party with friends costs nothing, and swapping by mail through a book-swap site runs about $5 a book in postage and fees. Take only what you’ll read, and bring your extras so the next swapper finds something latest.

A book you won’t read again still takes up shelf space, and the next one you want costs money.

It has been revealed that start with a Little Free Library, one of the small book boxes anyone can take from or add to. Little Free Library’s map and its free app show boxes near you, though only those their owners registered and chose to list. The organization’s rules don’t require you to leave a book to take one, but keeping a box stocked is up to the people who use it, so bring a few of yours.

In a recent development, for a specific title, try a book-swap site. On PaperBackSwap, open to U.S. residents over 18, each book you mail to a member who requests it earns a credit. Each credit gets you a paperback or hardcover that another member mails at their expense.

You pay to mail yours. A typical paperback weighs under a pound and costs $4.39 to send by Media Mail, the Postal Service’s low-cost option for books. PaperBackSwap’s free blueprint charges a 99-cent swap fee for each book you request, but printing your postage through the site costs 55 cents and earns you a request with no fee. That puts each book you get at about $4.94 in postage and fees.

For a swap party, ask friends or coworkers to bring books they’ve finished and would recommend. Set them out by genre, and draw numbers so people take turns picking one at a time. Donate the leftover books.

Say you have 12 finished paperbacks, each under a pound. Mailing six to PaperBackSwap members who request them, with postage printed through the site, costs $29.64, and the six credits you earn get you six books with no swap fees. Leave the other six in a Little Free Library box over a few visits and take six you’ll read. That’s 12 books you haven’t read for $29.64, about $2.47 each.

List 10 finished books on PaperBackSwap, and its two startup credits, which go to one account per household, get you two books before you mail any.

Pay Less for Amazon Prime – Get a Half-Price Blueprint or Share One Membership

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (436 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Moneycrashers

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Prime costs about half as much for anyone 18 to 24 or in college and for people on SNAP, Medicaid, or other qualifying aid, so check those looks before you pay $139 a year.
  • Both discounted intends carry the same core benefits as regular Prime, so paying the full $14.99 a month instead of $7.49 or $6.99 costs $90 to $96 more a year.
  • Industry observers note that prime Access costs $6.99 a month after a 30-day free trial for newly introduced members.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Prime costs about half as much for anyone 18 to 24 or in college and for people on SNAP, Medicaid, or other qualifying aid, so check those looks before you pay $139 a year. If another adult in your home also pays full price, cancel one membership and share the one you keep through Amazon Family.

Both discounted intends carry the same core benefits as regular Prime, so paying the full $14.99 a month instead of $7.49 or $6.99 costs $90 to $96 more a year.

Industry observers note that prime Access costs $6.99 a month after a 30-day free trial for newly introduced members. It’s open to people on SNAP, Medicaid, Social Security disability, or one of 10 other assistance programs, including public housing and energy aid, and to anyone who passes Amazon’s income check. You upload proof, such as your benefits card or eligibility letter, and reverify every 12 months.

On regular Prime or Prime for Young Adults, pay monthly only if you’ll keep the membership nine months or fewer, such as just for the holidays. Ten months of regular Prime at $14.99 cost $149.90, more than the $139 yearly price, so switch to yearly billing once you know you’ll keep it.

In a recent development, amazon Family, which replaced Amazon Household, lets a Prime member share free delivery, Prime Video, Amazon Music, and member deals with one other adult in the household, who keeps a separate Amazon account. Two adults paying $139 each can cancel one membership and save $139 a year.

Prime for Young Adults and free trials can’t be shared, so the shared membership has to be regular Prime or Prime Access. And the member who shares Prime must also share a payment method, which the other adult can use for purchases, so set this up only with someone you’d trust with it.

In a home where either adult qualifies for Prime Access, keep that membership, since it covers both of you for $83.88 a year, $55.12 less than one regular annual membership.

Read our Amazon Prime review to see whether the membership is worth its full price.
